title: Salary Claims: Check Source, Date and Role
description: Read India salary and hiring claims critically: check dates, job level, location, sample and base pay versus CTC before using a headline to plan your next move.
lead: Use these prompts to identify the evidence and questions that matter in your situation.
editorialFrame: Read a salary or hiring claim by checking its source, date, level, location, sample and definition. Keep market context separate from a written offer and never turn a headline into a personal pay promise.

sections.heading: A practical decision test
sections.content: For each headline, record publisher, publication date, geography, population, definition, sample and whether the source is primary or sponsored. Then write one conclusion the evidence supports and one it cannot support. Do not translate an aggregate trend into a personal pay expectation without role-specific evidence.

sections.heading: Evidence that should change your view
sections.content: Revisit the source when its population, date range, or definition changes. Keep a claim only if the underlying document is reachable and supports the wording you use. If the source cannot answer a question, mark it unknown instead of filling the gap with a converted headline or social post.

sections.heading: Build a claim record
sections.content:
Copy the exact wording and save the original source. Record who published it, when the data was collected, when the page was updated, which workers or employers are included and what the number means. A salary figure might describe base pay, total compensation, an advertised range or a self-reported amount. A hiring claim might count postings, survey responses, planned roles or completed hires. Those are different objects.

Check whether the source links to its method and sample. Look for exclusions, geography, job level, currency, time period and how duplicate postings are treated. If the article repeats a number but not the underlying research, trace it back. A company announcement can accurately describe that company's plan without establishing what the whole market will do.

sections.heading: Check comparability before interpreting
sections.content:
Compare like with like: role family, seniority, location, pay period, currency and whether the figure is base or CTC. If the source groups very different occupations, its average may not describe the role you are considering. If the sample is self-selected or limited to one employer, keep that boundary visible. Do not derive an individual probability from a sector total.

For salary, request a component-wise written offer and compare its defined amounts with your own current terms. The site's offer tool compares inputs; it does not verify a market benchmark or determine what an employer must pay. For hiring, look at current vacancies and ask what tasks the role covers. A count is a prompt for questions, not evidence that you personally can secure a specific role.

sections.heading: Illustrative scenarios and common traps
sections.content:
Illustrative scenario: A social post says salaries rose sharply but links only to a summary. The reader searches for the original report, finds no sample or pay definition and records the claim as unverified rather than using it in a negotiation.

Illustrative scenario: A headline reports many openings across a broad technology category. An applicant checks the location and seniority mix, then compares the roles with their own skills instead of dividing the total by all job seekers.

Illustrative scenario: Two offers display similar annual totals, but one includes variable pay and employer costs. The candidate asks for the breakup and uses the comparison tool only after entering comparable definitions.

Common errors include comparing gross with net, mixing old and current periods, quoting a range midpoint as an entitlement, and treating a forecast as completed hiring.

sections.heading: Keep a source trail
sections.content:
Use a small table with claim, source, publication and data dates, population, definition, caveat and your confidence. If a field is missing, write “not stated.” Check whether an update changed the underlying data or only the page text. Prefer primary reports or official datasets for factual claims, while recognizing that primary status does not make every conclusion universal.

Before repeating a statistic in a portfolio, interview or negotiation, verify that its wording matches the source and retain the link and capture date. If the source disappears, do not invent a replacement citation. Ask the employer for role-specific evidence and use the written offer for your own decision. A claim that cannot be scoped should remain a question, not a number presented as fact.

sections.heading: Questions to ask
sections.content: Ask who was counted, when data were collected, how “salary,” “job” or “growth” was defined, which locations and levels are included and what the source leaves out. For an offer, ask which components are guaranteed and how variable amounts are treated. Keep the original report, not only a social summary, alongside your comparison notes.

sections.heading: Check the claim before you repeat it
sections.content:
Before using a number in a presentation or interview, write a one-sentence version that includes its scope. If that sentence becomes too qualified to be useful, the source may not support the claim you hoped to make. Keep a note of whether the number was observed, projected, surveyed or advertised; never change one category into another for a stronger headline.

When two sources disagree, compare their definitions and collection periods before deciding that one is wrong. They may be describing different populations. Prefer the source that explains its method and matches the question, but keep uncertainty if no source resolves the difference. A saved link and date help another reader check your reasoning. Do not fill a missing methodology with an invented sample size or a convenient conversion.

sections.heading: Distinguish a market context from your negotiation
sections.content:
A market report can help you ask whether an offer is unusual, but it cannot show what an employer will pay for a particular scope or candidate. Compare written responsibilities, location, seniority and total package, then ask for the employer's pay band or level where appropriate. Do not present a broad mean as a legal minimum or an amount every peer receives.

If you share research in an interview, explain the source and caveat in the same breath. This signals that you can use evidence without overstating it. Keep a copy of the actual report and check whether the page has changed since you first read it. If a recruiter challenges the figure, return to the definition and sample rather than defending an unsourced summary.

nextSteps: Record who produced the figure, when it was published, which workers it covers, and what counts as a job or salary.
Check whether the underlying report is primary research, a company release, sponsored content, or a secondary summary.
Use an offer document and role-specific evidence for a personal decision; do not infer an individual outcome from a market total.

faqs.question: Is an advertised salary range a promise?
faqs.answer: No; confirm the written offer, level, components and conditions.

faqs.question: What does a hiring number need?
faqs.answer: A source, date, population, geography and clear definition of what was counted.

faqs.question: Can I use a market average to negotiate?
faqs.answer: Use it as context only after checking comparability; ask for role-specific terms.

faqs.question: What if the source has no method?
faqs.answer: Label the claim unverified and do not repeat it as established fact.
